claim: The Activity Recording CAFE (ARC) is a system that couples machine vision tracking of capillary-based food consumption and animal motion.
source: To simultaneously measure sleep and feeding of individual adult flies, we designed the Activity Recording CAFE (ARC), a system that couples machine vision tracking of capillary-based food consumption and animal motion (Figure 1A–C) (Ja et al., 2007; Donelson et al., 2012; Deshpande et al., 2014).
evidence: The manuscript describes the development and design of the ARC system with specific references to prior work.

claim: Flies inactive for 5 min exhibit multiple hallmarks of sleep.
source: Previous studies have shown that flies inactive for 5 min exhibit multiple hallmarks of sleep (Shaw et al., 2000; Huber et al., 2004; Hendricks et al., 2000).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: Sleep architecture in the ARC is similar to previous studies using high resolution object tracking.
source: Despite different housing and food consistency, we found sleep architecture to be similar to previous studies using high resolution object tracking, a method which has greater resolution of total sleep and sleep duration than the infrared-beam based alternative (Figure 1C, Figure 1—figure supplement 1A–D) (Donelson et al., 2012).
evidence: The claim is supported by comparison to previous studies and data shown in figures.

claim: Flies move less after meals than before, with the effect being more pronounced with larger meals.
source: Flies appeared to move less after meals than before—an effect more pronounced with larger meals—suggesting that sleep might also be greater after eating (Figure 1D).
evidence: The claim is supported by data shown in Figure 1D.

claim: Animals position themselves closer to food following each meal.
source: Animals also positioned themselves closer to the food following each meal (Figure 1E–F), consistent with observations that isolated flies sleep close to food (Hendricks et al., 2000) and the spatial tendency of flies driven to sleep by activation of neurons expressing short neuropeptide F, a satiety signaling hormone (Shang et al., 2013; Lee et al., 2004).
evidence: The claim is supported by data in figures and citations to previous studies.

claim: The probability of sleep (Psleep) declines sharply in the time approaching each meal.
source: The animals experienced a sharp decline in Psleep in the time approaching each meal, as expected since flies cannot sleep and feed simultaneously.
evidence: The claim is supported by data analysis and logical inference about the incompatibility of sleep and feeding.

claim: Psleep rises rapidly after a meal and exceeds the respective pre-meal Psleep.
source: Subsequent to the meal, Psleep rose rapidly and exceeded the respective pre-meal Psleep (Figure 2A).
evidence: The claim is supported by data shown in Figure 2A.

claim: Postprandial sleep lasts approximately 20–40 min with a maximum ΔPsleep amplitude of 0.15 and 0.2 for w1118 and Canton-S, respectively.
source: This analysis revealed a rise in sleep lasting approximately 20–40 min with a maximum ΔPsleep amplitude of 0.15 and 0.2 for the control strains, w1118 and Canton-S, respectively (Figure 2B).
evidence: The claim is supported by quantitative data analysis shown in Figure 2B.

claim: The postprandial sleep effect is observed in both males and females.
source: The effect was observed in both males and females (Figure 2—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: The claim is supported by data shown in a supplementary figure.

claim: Sleep initiation is more probable following a meal.
source: While the duration of sleep events prior to a meal is inherently limited by the time until an animal wakes to eat, sleep initiation is not limited and was more probable following a meal (Figure 2—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: The claim is supported by data shown in a supplementary figure.

claim: Arousal threshold initially increases with the amount of time that a fly is inactive, with the greatest change occurring in the first 5 min.
source: Consistent with previous studies, we found that arousal threshold initially increases with the amount of time that a fly is inactive, with the greatest change occurring in the first 5 min (Figure 2D) (Shaw et al., 2000; Huber et al., 2004; van Alphen et al., 2013; Faville et al., 2015).
evidence: The claim is supported by data in Figure 2D and citations to previous studies.

claim: Animals inactive for 0–5 min show a significantly greater arousal threshold in the 20, 40, and 60 min post-meal compared to respective pre-meal times.
source: In this transition state animals showed a significantly greater arousal threshold in the 20, 40, and 60 min post-meal compared to animals during the respective pre-meal times (Figure 2F).
evidence: The claim is supported by data shown in Figure 2F with statistical significance indicated.

claim: Food intake transiently influences sleep induction rather than depth.
source: This suggests that food intake transiently influences sleep induction rather than depth, which might be shaped solely by the amount of time that an animal is inactive.
evidence: The claim is based on inference from the correlation data between arousal threshold and postprandial sleep.

claim: Falsely calculated sleep due to grooming accounts for ~7% of sleep surrounding meals and has statistically indistinguishable occurrence before and after a meal.
source: Falsely calculated sleep, in which animals were grooming rather than immobile, accounted for ~7% of sleep surrounding meals and had statistically indistinguishable occurrence before and after a meal (Figure 2G, Figure 2—figure supplement 3).
evidence: The claim is supported by manual scoring data shown in figures.

claim: Re-analysis of sleep where sleep was defined as periods of immobility and lack of grooming exceeding 5 min lowered total sleep but did not alter the rise in postprandial sleep.
source: Re-analysis of sleep surrounding a meal, where sleep was defined as periods of immobility and a lack of grooming exceeding 5 min, lowered total sleep but did not alter the rise in postprandial sleep (Figure 2H).
evidence: The claim is supported by re-analysis data shown in Figure 2H.

claim: Sleep following meals increases as a function of meal size.
source: We plotted Psleep or ΔPsleep for different consumption volumes and found that sleep following meals increased as a function of meal size, while pre-prandial sleep did not (Figure 3A, Figure 3—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: The claim is supported by data shown in figures.

claim: There is a significant correlation between ΔPsleep and consumption volume when meals are analyzed individually or binned.
source: We found a significant correlation between ΔPsleep and consumption volume when meals were analyzed individually (Figure 3—figure supplement 1B) or binned (Figure 3B).
evidence: The claim is supported by correlation analysis shown in figures.

claim: The change in movement rate after a meal (Δspeed) shows a much weaker correlation to meal size than ΔPsleep.
source: The change in movement rate after a meal (Δspeed) showed a much weaker correlation to meal size than ΔPsleep (Figure 3—figure supplement 2C).
evidence: The claim is supported by correlation analysis shown in a supplementary figure.

claim: There is a highly significant correlation between meal volume and 20 min ΔPsleep.
source: We found a highly significant correlation between meal volume and 20 min ΔPsleep (Figure 4A, Figure 4—figure supplement 1A–B).
evidence: The claim is supported by correlation analysis shown in figures.

claim: ΔPsleep is significantly correlated to both protein and salt ingestion.
source: We found that ΔPsleep was significantly correlated to both protein and salt ingestion (Figure 4A, Figure 4—figure supplement 1A–B).
evidence: The claim is supported by correlation analysis shown in figures.

claim: There is no correlation between ingested sucrose and ΔPsleep.
source: Interestingly, despite reported effects of sucrose on total sleep (Keene et al., 2010; Linford et al., 2012), we found no correlation between ingested sucrose and ΔPsleep (Figure 4A, Figure 4—figure supplement 1A–B).
evidence: The claim is supported by correlation analysis shown in figures and contrasts with previous studies.

claim: Meal volume induces a greater rise in ΔPsleep amplitude than protein or salt for any given increase in total ΔPsleep during the decay.
source: For any given increase in total ΔPsleep during the decay, meal volume induced a greater rise in amplitude than protein or salt (Figure 4—figure supplement 2B).
evidence: The claim is supported by kinetic analysis shown in a supplementary figure.

claim: Silencing of Lkr neurons labeled by LkrGAL4 by overexpressing Kir2.1 eliminates any rise in postprandial sleep and instead causes slight arousal.
source: This manipulation eliminated any rise in postprandial sleep and instead caused slight arousal (Figure 5A).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5A.

claim: LkrGAL4 drives expression in neurons innervating the dorsal fan-shaped body, stemming from cell bodies in the lateral horn.
source: The expression pattern of LkrGAL4 recapitulates that of Lkr neurons which were found to regulate meal size (Al-Anzi et al., 2010), revealing several cell populations stemming from the lateral horn which innervate the dorsal fan-shaped body of the central complex—a region of the brain which functions in sleep homeostasis, visuomotor function, and hunger-related behavior (Figure 5B) (Donlea et al., 2011, 2014; Seelig and Jayaraman, 2013; Krashes et al., 2009).
evidence: The claim is supported by anatomical data shown in Figure 5B and citations to previous studies.

claim: LkrGAL4-silenced animals and their controls show similar ΔPsleep in response to ingested volume.
source: Silenced animals and their controls showed similar ΔPsleep in response to ingested volume, indicating that the LkrGAL4 neurons are not responsible for the volumetric modulation of postprandial sleep (Figure 5C).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5C.

claim: LkrGAL4-silenced animals and their controls show statistically indistinguishable ΔPsleep responses to salt manipulation.
source: LkrGAL4-silenced animals and their controls showed statistically indistinguishable ΔPsleep responses to salt manipulation (Figure 5D).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5D.

claim: While protein ingestion increases postprandial sleep in controls, LkrGAL4-silenced animals show a strong waking response.
source: In contrast, while protein ingestion increased postprandial sleep in controls, LkrGAL4-silenced animals showed a strong waking response, or a negative shift in postprandial sleep (Figure 5D).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5D.

claim: Protein can drive wakefulness in the absence of LkrGAL4 neuronal activity.
source: Interestingly, this waking response exceeded that of control animals on sucrose alone, indicating that protein can also drive wakefulness in the absence of LkrGAL4 neuronal activity.
evidence: The claim is based on inference from the experimental data comparing responses.

claim: Inactivation of GAL80ts to silence LkrGAL4-labeled cells in adulthood is sufficient to induce a postprandial sleep defect.
source: Inactivation of GAL80ts to silence LkrGAL4-labeled cells in adulthood was sufficient to induce a postprandial sleep defect (Figure 5F).
evidence: The claim is supported by conditional silencing data shown in Figure 5F.

claim: Immunostaining of Lk overlaps with LkGAL4-labeled cells in the lateral horn and in two cells in the suboesophageal ganglion (SOG).
source: Indeed, immunostaining of Lk overlapped with LkGAL4-labeled cells in the lateral horn, as well as in two cells in the suboesophageal ganglion (SOG) (Figure 6A).
evidence: The claim is supported by immunostaining data shown in Figure 6A.

claim: Thermogenetic activation of LkGAL4-labeled cells with TrpA significantly reduces postprandial sleep.
source: Using thermogenetic activation of these cells with the transient receptor potential channel TrpA, we found that postprandial sleep was significantly reduced upon activation (Figure 6B), furthering the notion that these cells inhibit Lkr neurons.
evidence: The claim is supported by thermogenetic activation data shown in Figure 6B.

claim: Knockdown of Lk in LkGAL4-labeled cells using two independent RNAi lines increases postprandial sleep.
source: We found that this knockdown increased postprandial sleep, consistent with the idea that expression of Lk in LkGAL4-labeled cells is necessary for the inhibitory effect on Lkr neuronal activity (Figure 6C).
evidence: The claim is supported by RNAi knockdown data shown in Figure 6C.

claim: 20G03 labels cell bodies in the lateral horn and SOG, as well as a subset of mushroom body output neurons (MBONs).
source: R20G03 (20G03), a line expressing GAL4 driven by an enhancer fragment 316 base pairs upstream of Lk, labels cell bodies in the lateral horn and SOG, as well as a subset of mushroom body output neurons (MBONs) (Figure 7A), all of which coincide with Lkr neurons labeled by the LkrGAL4driver (Figure 7B).
evidence: The claim is supported by anatomical data shown in Figures 7A and 7B.

claim: The cholinergic MBONs of 20G03 play a role in short-term appetitive memory following food intake.
source: The cholinergic MBONs of 20G03 have been shown to play a role in short-term appetitive memory following food intake (Aso et al., 2014).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to a previous study.

claim: Constitutive and adult-restricted silencing of 20G03 neurons increases postprandial sleep.
source: To test this, we again employed electrical silencing with Kir2.1 and found that constitutive and adult-restricted silencing of these neurons increased postprandial sleep, suggesting that these cells might directly inhibit the activity of proximal Lkr neurons (Figure 7C–D).
evidence: The claim is supported by silencing data shown in Figures 7C and 7D.

claim: Immunostaining of Lk does not co-localize with any of the 20G03 cells.
source: Interestingly, immunostaining of Lk did not co-localize with any of the 20G03 cells, nor did downregulation of Lk in these cells affect postprandial sleep (Figure 7—figure supplement 1A–B), suggesting that their inhibitory action stems from an alternative neuropeptide or neurotransmitter.
evidence: The claim is supported by immunostaining and RNAi data shown in supplementary figures.

claim: The increase in postprandial sleep driven by 20G03 silencing is most pronounced at ZT 12.
source: By analyzing behavior throughout a 24 hr period, we found that the increase in postprandial sleep driven by 20G03 silencing was most pronounced at ZT 12 (Figure 7E–F).
evidence: The claim is supported by time-course analysis shown in Figures 7E and 7F.

claim: 20G03 silencing increases sleep after but not before each meal within ZT 10–14.
source: Closer examination within this period showed that, rather than raising sleep evenly within ZT 10–14, the sleep after but not before each meal was increased (Figure 7G), implying that these cells activate in response to food intake.
evidence: The claim is supported by detailed analysis shown in Figure 7G and inference about cell activation.

claim: The ARC is the first platform capable of simultaneously measuring sleep and resolving discrete feeding events in individual flies.
source: The ARC is the first platform capable of simultaneously measuring sleep and resolving discrete feeding events in individual flies.
evidence: This is a direct statement about the novelty of the ARC system.

claim: Flies exhibit a rise in sleep following a meal.
source: Using this tool, we found that flies exhibit a rise in sleep following a meal.
evidence: This is a summary statement of the main finding supported by data throughout the manuscript.

claim: Consumption of a meal does not necessarily affect the depth of sleep when controlling for time inactive.
source: Interestingly, consumption of a meal did not necessarily affect the depth of sleep when controlling for time inactive.
evidence: This is based on analysis of arousal threshold data controlling for inactivity duration.

claim: Sleep probability and sleep depth can be dissociated.
source: Similarly, our work suggests that sleep probability and sleep depth can also be dissociated.
evidence: This is an inference based on the finding that meal consumption affects sleep probability but not depth.

claim: Cranial EEG power increases with meal size and during certain stages of sleep in humans.
source: This may be paralleled in humans where cranial EEG power increases with meal size and during certain stages of sleep (Reyner et al., 2012).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to a human study.

claim: Artificial distension of the gut increases sleep in rats.
source: While human studies have been unable to resolve a link between meal volume and measures of wakefulness (Landström et al., 2001), artificial distension of the gut has been shown to increase sleep in rats (Lorenz et al., 1998).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: Protein consumption modulates sleep in Drosophila and positively correlates with napping in humans.
source: Although there are no studies on the effect of protein on postprandial sleep, protein consumption modulates sleep in Drosophila and positively correlates with napping in humans (Catterson et al., 2010; Grandner et al., 2010).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: Salt intake increases mammalian oxytocin signaling, which has been implicated in sleep-wake behavior.
source: Similarly, although there are no studies on the influence of salt on postprandial sleep, salt intake increases mammalian oxytocin signaling, which has been implicated in sleep-wake behavior (Krause et al., 2011; Lancel et al., 2003).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: Sucrose plays a critical role in long-term sleep homeostasis and architecture in flies.
source: Sucrose has been shown to play a critical role in long-term sleep homeostasis and architecture in flies (Keene et al., 2010; Linford et al., 2012), although our findings indicate that it does not modulate postprandial sleep.
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous studies and contrasted with the current findings.

claim: The Lk system plays a role in postprandial sleep.
source: We demonstrate that the Lk system plays a role in postprandial sleep (Figure 7H).
evidence: This is a summary statement supported by multiple experiments throughout the manuscript.

claim: A subset of Lkr neurons is necessary to initiate postprandial sleep in the presence of protein.
source: A subset of Lkr neurons were necessary to initiate postprandial sleep in the presence of protein.
evidence: This is based on the silencing experiments showing that LkrGAL4 neurons are required for protein-induced postprandial sleep.

claim: Ingested protein promotes both sleep and wakefulness, and the wakefulness is normally counterbalanced by Lkr neuronal activity.
source: This suggests that ingested protein promotes both sleep and wakefulness, and that the wakefulness is normally counterbalanced by Lkr neuronal activity.
evidence: This is an inference based on the observation that LkrGAL4-silenced animals show a waking response to protein.

claim: Translin acts through Lk-expressing cells to drive wakefulness in response to sucrose starvation.
source: While this study does not specifically identify the waking output for protein, it was previously shown that Translin acts through Lk-expressing cells to drive wakefulness in response to sucrose starvation (Murakami et al., 2016).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to a previous study.

claim: Lkr neurons are circadian output neurons that modulate activity rhythmically.
source: Another recent finding identified Lkr neurons as circadian output neurons, which modulate activity rhythmically.
evidence: This claim is based on a recent finding, though the specific citation is not provided in this sentence.

claim: Incubation of Lkr cells with Lk shunts their calcium response to the cholinergic agonist carbachol.
source: The same study found that incubation of Lkr cells with Lk shunts their calcium response to the cholinergic agonist carbachol (Cavey et al., 2016), suggesting an inhibitory connection between Lk and downstream Lkr neurons.
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to a previous study.

claim: Stimulation of Lk neurons reduces postprandial sleep, matching the effect of Lkr silencing.
source: By stimulating these same Lk neurons, we observed a reduction of postprandial sleep matching the effect of Lkr silencing, providing additional evidence that the lateral horn harbors an inhibitory node between Lk and Lkr neurons.
evidence: This is based on the thermogenetic activation experiments shown in Figure 6B.

claim: Knockdown of Lk in LkGAL4-labeled cells increases postprandial sleep, supporting the notion of an inhibitory connection.
source: We also found that knockdown of Lk in these cells increased postprandial sleep, supporting this notion.
evidence: This is based on the RNAi experiments shown in Figure 6C.

claim: A subset of cells labeled by 20G03 modulates postprandial sleep during the period near 'dusk' or 'lights-off'.
source: We also found a subset of cells labeled by 20G03 that modulate postprandial sleep during the period near 'dusk' or 'lights-off'.
evidence: This is based on the time-course analysis shown in Figures 7E-F.

claim: The subset of 20G03 cells harbors acetylcholine MBONs that are necessary for short-term associative memory between sucrose consumption after starvation and an odor.
source: Interestingly, the subset harbors acetylcholine MBONs—cells necessary for the short-term associative memory between sucrose consumption after starvation and an odor (Aso et al., 2014).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to a previous study.

claim: 20G03 cells activate following a feeding event.
source: This suggests that these cells activate following a feeding event, in agreement with our results.
evidence: This is an inference based on the observation that silencing these cells increases postprandial but not pre-meal sleep.

claim: The tachykinin family to which Lk belongs has been implicated in the regulation of satiety and sleep.
source: The tachykinin family to which Lk belongs has been implicated in the regulation of satiety and sleep, however any physiological connections between these behavioral outputs has not been explored (Massi et al., 1988; Zielinski et al., 2015).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: The orexin system is regulated by a diversity of signaling molecules.
source: The orexin system is regulated by a diversity of signaling molecules (Scammell and Winrow, 2011) and has already shown promise as a target for sleep therapeutics.
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to a previous study.

claim: The ARC provides a platform for future studies aimed at uncovering additional genes, circuitry, and physiological roles of postprandial sleep.
source: Accordingly, the ARC provides a platform for future studies aimed at uncovering additional genes, circuitry, and physiological roles of postprandial sleep.
evidence: This is a statement about the potential applications of the ARC system.

claim: The ability to measure both sleep and feeding in individual animals may shed new light on the fundamental relationship between these behaviors in other paradigms.
source: Furthermore, the ability to measure both sleep and feeding in individual animals may shed new light on the fundamental relationship between these behaviors in other paradigms.
evidence: This is a speculative statement about future applications.
